html:
Cáhita is an umbrella name for several Indigenous peoples of the Pacific coast of northwest Mexico, in Sinaloa and Sonora, who spoke closely related Uto-Aztecan languages. They include the Yaqui, the Mayo and the Tehueco.

They lived in farming villages along the lower Yaqui, Mayo, Fuerte and Sinaloa rivers, growing maize, beans and squash on the floodplains, and fished and gathered along the coast. They were among the most numerous peoples of the northwest when the Spanish came, and fought off early expeditions. From the 1590s Jesuit missionaries founded missions among them and wrote down much of what is known of their life. The name Cáhita itself is said to come from a word meaning "nothing", given as an answer to missionaries. Their neighbours to the south included the Tahue.
